text: Immigration is usually sold as a simple meritocracy.
Move to a rich country,
study hard, get a good job, fit in.
But look at it through game theory, and
a different picture appears.
Immigration isn't a neutral elevator.
It's a game, and the rules were written
by the people already in charge.
Start with a puzzle.
Students from East Asian education systems top the
world's pizza rankings.
East Asian Americans have some of the highest
median incomes in the United States, and fill
engineering,
medicine,
and tech.
Yet research on corporate leadership keeps finding the
same thing, they are heavily underrepresented in the
executive suite.
People call it the bamboo ceiling.
Studies of some large dating platforms have found
a similar penalty,
with East Asian men receiving fewer replies than
other groups.
The lesson of game theory, doing everything right
by the rules, does not mean you control
the system.
Think of a casino,
bright lights, free drinks, the feeling of a
fair chance.
But if the games were truly fair, the
house would go broke.
The house sets the rules so the average
player loses,
and the casino keeps the money.
A country that opens its doors to global
talent plays a similar role.
You are invited to play, but the game
is built around the home team's norms,
communication style, and social networks.
Follow the rules,
pay taxes,
obey the law, work hard,
stay quiet.
You become a reliable contributor, but contributors are
not automatically the people who write the rules.
Play strictly by the rules, and you can
trade your skills for a paycheck, while staying
outside the rooms where status is decided.
Now zoom out.
Game theory says groups with strong trust and
cooperation often win repeated games.
Networks, mentors,
favors, and loyalty are how status actually moves.
That is the real trade -off,
dissolve into the crowd, and you may lose
your network.
Stay tightly inside your own community, and you
may stay outside everyone else's.
Population matters too, but the numbers are less
dramatic than people think.
Fertility has fallen below the replacement level of
about 2.1 children per woman across much
of the rich world,
and in most countries,
immigrant fertility drifts toward the local average within
a generation or two.
Forecasts for 2050 are guesses built on assumptions
about migration and birth rates.
Game theory can explain incentives.
It cannot predict who ends up running a
country.
Migration is not a modern invention, and it
was rarely gentle.
Ancient DNA shows early farmers spreading across Europe
and later step herders arriving and reshaping the
population,
sometimes through conquest,
sometimes through mixing.
Modern open immigration is recent.
It grew out of European expansion,
and then, after World War II,
American -led globalization built to fill labor shortages
and power industrial growth.
Systems like that tend to last only while
they serve the people who design them.
For developing countries there is a price,
brain drain,
doctors,
engineers and founders are told success means leaving
to look for money and respect in a
richer country's cities.
And some who go find that comfort comes
with a glass ceiling.
A big salary under someone else's rules is
not the same as power.
Real power comes from building,
shaping and sustaining institutions of your own.
So here is the sobering takeaway of the
game theory of immigration.
Whoever sets the rules tends to collect the
spoils.
For individuals and for nations,
the winning move is not climbing a rigged
ladder forever.
It is knowing when to build a game
of your own.
If you have lived this, what did the
rules cost you and what did they give
you?
Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe for the next game theory breakdown.
